problemText: Which of the following is a CENTRAL IDEA rather than just a topic?
choices: Bees produce honey that lasts a very long time because it contains very little water and is highly acidic.
Honey is a food made by bees from flower nectar and pollen, which represents one of nature's most useful products.
The ways that honey can stay fresh for many years involves understanding its chemical composition and storage conditions.
Stories about ancient honey jars found inside Egyptian tombs demonstrate how long this substance can survive without modern refrigeration.
hints: A central idea is a complete sentence that makes a claim, not just a word or short phrase.
The correct answer explains WHY something is true, not just WHAT the text is about.

problemText: Read this paragraph: "Penguins have flippers instead of wings that can fly through the air. These flippers are perfect for pushing a penguin through water very fast, the way airplane wings push through air. A penguin's flippers also help it steer and stop while swimming." Which sentence best states the central idea of this paragraph?
choices: Penguins have flippers.
Penguins' flippers are built to help them move, steer, and stop in the water.
Penguins' flippers work in water the way airplane wings work in air.
Penguins can swim very fast.
hints: Look for a sentence that covers ALL the different jobs the paragraph describes the flippers doing, not just one.
The central idea should explain the main point across the whole paragraph, not focus on only one detail like the comparison to airplanes.

problemText: A student reads a passage about how coral reefs protect coastlines from hurricanes and storm waves. The passage also mentions that coral reefs provide food and shelter for thousands of fish species. The student writes: "Coral reefs are important ecosystems." Why is this sentence NOT a good central idea for this passage?
choices: It is too short to be a central idea because central ideas must always be longer than one sentence.
It uses the word 'important' which is not specific enough to explain what the passage actually says about coral reefs, leaving out the particular benefits mentioned.
It does not cover the specific ways the passage explains that coral reefs matter, such as protecting coastlines and housing sea life.
It fails to mention the storm waves and hurricanes that are the main focus of the entire passage.
hints: A central idea needs to be broad enough to cover every main point the text makes, not so vague that it could mean almost anything.
Think about what the passage actually DOES say coral reefs do — not just that they are important, but HOW they matter.

problemText: Read this passage, then identify which statement is the CENTRAL IDEA and which is a SUPPORTING DETAIL that proves it. "Monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles each year as they migrate south for the winter. Along the way, they must find milkweed plants to lay their eggs on, because monarch caterpillars only eat milkweed leaves. When milkweed becomes harder to find because of farming or development, the butterflies have fewer safe places to raise their young. Scientists worry that without enough milkweed, the monarch population will continue to decline."
choices: The central idea is 'Monarch caterpillars only eat milkweed leaves,' and a supporting detail is 'Scientists worry that without enough milkweed, the monarch population will continue to decline.'
The central idea is 'Monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles each year,' and a supporting detail is 'Along the way, they must find milkweed plants to lay their eggs on.'
The central idea is 'Milkweed plants are disappearing because of farming and development,' and a supporting detail is 'Monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles each year.'
The central idea is 'The loss of milkweed threatens monarchs because they need it to reproduce and raise their young,' and a supporting detail is 'Monarch caterpillars only eat milkweed leaves.'
hints: The central idea should connect the two biggest ideas the passage keeps returning to: milkweed's disappearance AND why monarchs need it.
Look for a central idea that explains WHY the loss of milkweed is a problem, not just WHAT is happening or WHERE monarchs travel.

problemText: A student writes the following central idea: "Jellyfish do not have brains or hearts." She finds these two facts in her passage: (1) "Jellyfish lack a centralized brain and nervous system." (2) "Jellyfish are over 90 percent water." Does the second fact actually support her central idea? Explain why or why not.
choices: No, because being 90 percent water is a true fact about jellyfish but does not explain why jellyfish do not have brains or hearts.
Yes, because when jellyfish are made mostly of water, they cannot develop the organs that land animals need to survive.
Yes, because both facts are found in the passage and both describe unusual characteristics of how jellyfish are built and structured.
No, because the 90 percent water fact is too small and minor to count as a detail that supports any central idea at all.
hints: A supporting detail must connect directly to the central idea and help prove it is true.
Ask yourself: does knowing that jellyfish are 90 percent water help explain why they have no brains or hearts? Or is it a different fact entirely?

problemText: Read this passage: "The Great Barrier Reef stretches over 1,400 miles and contains thousands of coral species. Most coral species can only live in warm, shallow saltwater, where sunlight reaches the ocean floor. Coral also depends on tiny algae that live inside its cells and provide food through photosynthesis. When water temperature rises even a few degrees because of climate change, the algae die, and the coral turns white and dies soon after. Scientists have documented massive coral bleaching events occurring more frequently in recent decades." A student proposes this central idea: "The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef in the world." Use the two-detail test to explain whether this central idea works for the passage.
choices: The central idea works because the passage opens by describing the reef's size and location, which serves as the foundation for all the other information presented.

The central idea does not work because although the passage mentions the reef's size once, most of the passage explains what coral needs to survive and why it is dying, not why the Great Barrier Reef is large.
The central idea works because it is supported by the fact that the reef contains thousands of coral species and also by the documented bleaching events that show it is under threat.
The central idea does not work because the passage does not explicitly state that the Great Barrier Reef is larger than every other coral reef in existence.
hints: Try the two-detail test: can you find two separate facts in the passage that explain WHY the reef is the largest? Or do most of the passage's details point to a different main idea?
Remember: a central idea must be broad enough to cover what the passage keeps returning to across nearly all its paragraphs, not just what appears in the opening sentence.

problemText: A marine biologist observes the bioluminescence, the ability of certain organisms to produce light through a chemical reaction inside their bodies, in deep-sea fish. What does bioluminescence mean as used in this passage?
choices: A type of reflection that occurs when moonlight bounces off the ocean surface during nighttime hours
The scientific study of how different wavelengths of light travel and refract through seawater
The ability of certain organisms to produce light through a chemical reaction inside their bodies
The natural luminescence that results when organisms consume and metabolize their food sources
hints: Look right after the technical term for a restatement set off by a comma or dash.
Use exactly what the passage tells you, not what you might guess about the word.

problemText: A chef explains that to achieve the perfect emulsion, the thick mixture that forms when oil and vinegar are beaten together into a smooth blend, you must whisk the ingredients slowly and steadily. If the chef's emulsion separates and becomes thin and watery again, which of these is most likely to have happened?
choices: The chef used vinegar and oil from different suppliers than what was used previously
The chef added an ingredient that prevented the oil and vinegar from combining into the thick, smooth blend required for an emulsion
The chef selected a bowl made from material that did not have the right surface texture for whisking
The oil and vinegar stopped being beaten together into a smooth blend
hints: Swap the definition of emulsion back into the sentence about what happened when it separated.
The definition tells you exactly what an emulsion is—so when it stops being that, what must have gone wrong?

problemText: A meteorologist describes the formation of precipitation, such as rain, sleet, and snow that falls from clouds. Later in the same text, the meteorologist mentions that "water droplets inside the cloud continue to grow until they become heavy enough to fall as precipitation." Based on the passage, which of these is an example of precipitation?
choices: Hail that falls from a storm cloud
A mist that hovers just above the ground without falling
Frost that forms on a window during a cold night
Dew that appears on grass in the early morning
hints: Look for the example clue words—the passage uses 'such as' to show what precipitation includes.
Remember the definition tells you precipitation falls from clouds—check which choice actually falls that way.

problemText: A student read this sentence: "The captain ordered the crew to trim the ballast, the heavy material carried in the bottom of a ship to keep it stable in rough water." The student's classmate said ballast means "a small ball used in games." Why is the classmate's answer wrong, and what should the classmate have done instead?
choices: The classmate chose a meaning that appears in dictionaries but never applies to anything related to ships, so technical definitions never vary based on the subject being discussed
The classmate borrowed an everyday meaning instead of reading the restatement the passage provided; the correct meaning is the heavy material carried in the bottom of a ship to keep it stable
The classmate overlooked the comma that signals a restatement is coming, even though passages always use punctuation marks like commas and dashes to introduce definitions for technical terms
The classmate failed to use context clues before consulting the definition, even though most passages do not actually include direct definitions for specialized vocabulary words
hints: Think about the everyday-meaning trap—what meaning did the classmate already know before reading?
The passage gives a signal right after the technical term—what does that signal tell you to do?

problemText: A geologist writes: "The plateau, a flat-topped landform that rises abruptly from the surrounding terrain, covers thousands of square miles in that region. From the air, the plateau looks like a giant table sitting on top of the land." Which statement best explains why the second sentence helps confirm your understanding of plateau?
choices: It provides a specific example by naming the exact geographic region where the plateau is located and explaining how the surrounding terrain differs from it
It restates the scientific definition word-for-word to reinforce the technical vocabulary and ensure the reader memorizes all the key terms introduced in the first sentence
It offers a comparison that matches the key feature named in the restatement—something flat and elevated that looks different from the land around it
It introduces a visual image that simplifies the concept by comparing the plateau to familiar household furniture, allowing readers to imagine how the landform actually appears from above
hints: The first sentence has a restatement—what key features does it name?
Does the second sentence add a completely new definition, or does it help you picture what 'flat-topped' and 'rises abruptly' actually look like?

problemText: A naturalist writes: "To study the canopy—the continuous layer of leaves and branches formed by the highest trees in a forest—researchers often must climb or use rope bridges positioned high in the treetops. Some canopies are so thick that almost no sunlight reaches the forest floor." A student concludes that 'canopy' means 'the rope bridges used by researchers.' Why is this conclusion wrong, and what error did the student make when reading for the technical term's meaning?
choices: The student remembered the everyday meaning of canopy and applied it instead of trusting the definition the passage printed
The student looked for example clues using words like 'such as' but did not notice the restatement signal that comes before them
The student correctly identified the technical term but swapped back the wrong meaning and did not check whether the sentence would still make sense
The student found the restatement in dashes but confused a supporting detail mentioned elsewhere in the passage with the actual definition provided
hints: The student picked out something from the passage that is connected to canopy but is not the definition itself—what is that something, and where is the real definition?
What comes right after 'canopy' in dashes, and does a rope bridge match that description?

problemText: A textbook page about the water cycle has four sections, each with its own heading: 'Evaporation', 'Condensation', 'Precipitation', and 'Collection'. What is the main job of these headings?
choices: They establish that evaporation is the most critical stage and must be studied before learning about condensation, precipitation, and collection.
They give detailed explanations of how water moves from the ocean through clouds and returns to the ground in a continuous cycle.
They tell the reader which stages of the water cycle occur simultaneously and depend on each other at the same moment in time.
They divide the page into separate topics so a reader can see which section covers which part of the water cycle and find the one they need.
hints: Think about what a heading does before you read the paragraph — does it tell you the answer, or does it tell you where to look?
A heading is a short label. What does a reader learn from seeing all four headings together, before reading any paragraph?

problemText: An article about desert plants has a paragraph that reads: 'A saguaro cactus stores water in its thick, waxy skin so it can survive months without rain. The plant grows very slowly, adding only a few inches per year.' Below this paragraph is a photograph of a large saguaro cactus. The caption under the photograph reads: 'This saguaro cactus in Arizona is over 150 years old.' Which piece of information does the caption add that is not already in the paragraph?
choices: A specific location and age for one particular saguaro cactus
That saguaro cacti have thick, waxy skin to store water
That saguaro cacti grow very slowly
That saguaro cacti can survive for a long time without rain
hints: Cover the caption with your thumb. Is the paragraph missing a location or an age?
The paragraph talks about saguaro cacti in general. What does the caption pin down that the paragraph left vague?

problemText: A magazine section on coral reefs includes a main paragraph and a boxed sidebar titled 'Did You Know?' The paragraph explains that coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps and that reefs are home to thousands of fish and plant species. The sidebar reads: 'The world's largest coral reef, the Great Barrier Reef, stretches for over 1,400 miles along the coast of Australia.' If a reader skipped the sidebar and read only the main paragraph, what would they still understand about coral reefs?
choices: That the Great Barrier Reef is in Australia and is over 1,400 miles long
That coral reefs are made of tiny animals and support many kinds of sea life
How large individual coral polyps are and how they attach to the ocean floor
That coral reefs are the most important ecosystems on Earth
hints: The sidebar is boxed off to the side. A reader who skips it misses one thing — what is that one thing?
The paragraph covers the basic facts about what coral reefs are and what lives in them. Is that enough for the reader to understand the main point without the sidebar?

problemText: A science article about the human skeleton has a section titled 'How Bones Heal'. The paragraph reads: 'When a bone breaks, the body immediately begins to mend it. New bone tissue forms in and around the break within days. Over weeks and months, the new tissue hardens and grows stronger until it is as tough as the original bone.' Below the paragraph is a labeled diagram showing a broken bone at different stages: Day 1 (the break), Day 10 (new tissue forming), and Month 3 (the bone healed). The caption under the diagram reads: 'The healing process happens in stages over time.' Why does this diagram contribute something important to understanding this section that the paragraph alone does not make equally clear?
choices: The diagram shows the visual appearance of new tissue forming at each stage, which helps readers see what happens at Day 1, Day 10, and Month 3 all together in one view
The diagram proves the paragraph's information is accurate by providing evidence from scientific research studies

The diagram shows exactly how much time passes between each stage of healing and displays all the stages side by side in one view, whereas the paragraph describes the stages one after another in words
The diagram explains exactly how bone cells multiply during healing, whereas the paragraph only describes the general process of hardening and strengthening
hints: Ask what the diagram lets a reader see in one glance that the paragraph's sentences would need several sentences to show.
The paragraph describes the healing steps in order, one at a time. How is seeing them all at once in a picture different from reading about them in sentences?

problemText: An article about rainforests has a section titled 'The Canopy Layer' with this paragraph: 'The canopy is the thick layer of leaves and branches formed by the tallest trees in the rainforest. It sits so high and is so dense that very little sunlight reaches the plants below it. Many animals, including monkeys, jaguars, and birds, live their entire lives in the canopy without ever touching the forest floor.' Beside the paragraph is a sidebar labeled 'Canopy Facts' that says: 'The canopy layer can be over 100 feet above the ground. Some scientists estimate that half of all rainforest animal species live in the canopy.' Using the thumb test, identify what the sidebar contributes to this section.
choices: It explains the reasons why monkeys, jaguars, and birds prefer to live in the canopy rather than spending time on the forest floor below
It provides specific measurements of height and population percentages that support and expand on the paragraph's description of the canopy
It describes what the canopy looks like by explaining the colors and shapes of the leaves and branches that form this layer
It adds specific details about the canopy's height and how many animal species depend on it, which the main paragraph does not provide
hints: Cover the sidebar with your thumb and reread the paragraph. What fact or number does the paragraph not include?
The paragraph tells you what the canopy is and that animals live there. What numbers or specific comparisons does only the sidebar give?

problemText: A page about bees has two sections. The first section, titled 'How Bees Make Honey', includes a paragraph and a flow-chart graphic showing the steps: flower visits → pollen collected → pollen brought to hive → nectar processed → honey stored. The second section, titled 'Why Bees Need Nectar', has a paragraph explaining that nectar contains natural sugars that give bees the energy they need to fly and work, and a caption under a photograph that reads: 'Worker bees can fly up to 55 miles per day to find flowers.' A student is trying to decide which text feature in the first section — the heading or the graphic — contributes the most new information that the paragraph alone does not clearly show. What is the strongest reason for choosing the graphic over the heading?
choices: The heading only names the topic, but the graphic shows the actual sequence of steps and how they connect to each other, which a paragraph listing the steps one at a time would be harder to hold in your mind all at once
The graphic displays each step in a visual format using arrows and boxes, which takes up less space on the page than writing out all the steps in sentence form would
The graphic reveals additional facts about how long each step takes and the temperature needed for nectar to turn into honey, details that the paragraph does not include
The heading tells readers only what the section is about, but the graphic shows the exact relationship between steps and demonstrates how one step leads to the next in a clear sequence
hints: What is the difference between a heading's job and a graphic's job? What does each one do that the other does not?
A heading names what the section covers. A graphic shows what would take multiple sentences to describe. Which one shows the relationship between steps?

problemText: A student is writing an objective summary of an informational passage about how plants grow roots. Which of the following should the student include in the summary?
choices: Every fact from the passage in the exact order it appeared
The central idea of the passage and only the details that support it
The central idea plus the student's own opinion about how interesting roots are
A retelling of the passage that treats all facts as equally important
hints: Think about what 'objective' means and what an objective summary leaves out.
Remember that a summary is shorter than a retelling because it drops facts that don't connect to the main idea.

problemText: Read this sentence from a student's summary: 'This shows that bees are incredibly intelligent at organizing their hives.' The student is trying to write an objective summary about how bees organize their hives. What is the problem with this sentence, and how should the student fix it?
choices: The sentence presents facts in a different order than they appeared in the passage, mixing up the sequence of events that describe how bees actually build and maintain their hives
The sentence skips important details from the passage and omits specific information about the methods bees use to organize their living spaces and perform their tasks
The sentence uses a judgment word, 'incredibly,' and announces a conclusion with 'this shows that' instead of reporting what the passage actually says about how bees organize
The sentence fails to identify what aspect of bee behavior is most important and does not explain the central point that the passage is trying to communicate about hives
hints: Look for the quiet kind of judgment—words that hand over the summarizer's own opinion, not just obvious words like 'amazing.'
An objective summary reports facts from the passage, not what the summarizer thinks about those facts.

problemText: A passage explains that butterflies taste with their feet to find food plants. A student writes this summary: 'Butterflies have feet. Butterflies can taste. Butterflies use their sense of taste to find food plants. Butterflies live in many places.' Which supporting detail should be removed from this summary?
choices: The detail 'Butterflies have feet' is background information that doesn't directly connect to the main idea about how butterflies locate the specific plants they need to eat
The detail 'Butterflies can taste' restates information already included in the next sentence and therefore adds no new understanding about how butterflies find food plants
The detail 'Butterflies use their sense of taste to find food plants' should not be removed since it directly supports and explains the central idea of the entire summary
'Butterflies live in many places' does not connect to how butterflies taste with their feet to find food
hints: A supporting detail must explain or prove the central idea, not just be any true fact about the topic.
Ask yourself: does this detail help explain why or how butterflies taste with their feet to find food?

problemText: A student is summarizing a passage about how deserts stay dry. The passage explains that mountains block rain clouds, that air in deserts is warm and holds less moisture, and that deserts rarely get visitors. The central idea has already been identified: deserts form where mountains block rain or where warm air cannot hold moisture. Which fact from the passage should the student keep, and which should be dropped?
choices: Keep both the mountain detail and the warm air detail because both support the central idea; drop the detail about visitors because it does not explain why deserts stay dry
Keep only the mountain detail and drop the warm air detail since the mountain blocking rain is the primary reason that all deserts in the world receive such little precipitation and moisture
Drop both the mountain detail and the warm air detail, and keep the visitor detail instead because it emphasizes how extreme desert conditions are and shows that deserts are inhabitable places
Keep the visitor detail because it appears at the end of the passage and the warm air detail since it is mentioned second, dropping only the mountain detail as less relevant
hints: Every supporting detail in your summary must connect back to the central idea you are building, not just be true or interesting.
Think about what the passage is really trying to explain—why deserts are dry—and keep only the details that answer that question.

problemText: A passage describes how tornadoes form: warm, moist air rises, cool air pushes down, the air layers spin, and a tornado funnel appears. A student writes this summary: 'Warm, moist air is present. Cool air moves downward. When these air layers spin together, a tornado funnel forms. This proves that nature's power is frightening.' The central idea is: tornadoes form when warm, moist air and cool air create spinning layers that become a funnel. Identify two problems with the student's summary and explain how to fix both.
choices: The summary is unnecessarily long and repetitive because it lists every single detail from the passage separately instead of combining them into shorter and more efficient sentences without losing meaning

The summary repeats facts as separate sentences instead of combining them into one, and it ends with a judgment using 'proves' that states the summarizer's own reaction instead of reporting the passage
The summary fails to mention that the passage discusses rising and sinking air movements and it incorrectly changes the order of tornado formation steps from what the passage describes in sequence

The summary omits the explanation that warm air must rise higher than cool air and it includes personal feelings about nature that contradict the factual information the passage provides about meteorology
hints: Look for two separate mistakes: one about how a summary is written (how many sentences, how details are combined) and one about staying objective.
Remember that the last sentence of the student's summary announces what the summarizer thinks about tornadoes, not what the passage says.

problemText: A passage explains that salt dissolves in water because water molecules pull the salt apart, that dissolving salt is useful for melting ice on roads, that salt has been mined for thousands of years, and that dissolved salt can be separated from water by heating. A student is writing an objective summary. The central idea is: salt dissolves in water because water molecules pull the salt crystal apart into separate pieces. The student has written three possible summaries below. Which one correctly includes only details that support the central idea, stays objective, and is noticeably shorter than the original passage without retelling it sentence by sentence?
choices: Salt dissolves in water because water molecules pull the salt crystal apart. This process is useful in many ways.
Water molecules pull salt crystals apart, which causes salt to dissolve. People have mined salt for thousands of years.
Salt dissolves when water molecules pull the crystal apart into separate pieces. Separated salt can be recovered by heating the water.
Salt dissolves in water as water molecules pull the crystal apart. Salt has been used for thousands of years because it dissolves.
hints: Check each choice: does it state the central idea, include only details that explain WHY salt dissolves, stay objective (no judgment words or conclusion-announcing phrases), and avoid retelling?

The detail about heating water to separate dissolved salt supports the central idea by showing what happens after dissolution, but facts about usefulness or ancient mining do not explain the dissolving process itself.
